metaDescription: Need a sharp prompt for Gemini? Copy ready-made ones above for summaries, drafts, and Nano Banana photo edits, then tweak each to fit your own work fast.
bodyHtml:
A prompt for Gemini is the instruction you type into Google's AI, and the distance between a lazy one and a sharp one is enormous. Gemini really does two jobs that feel like different apps. It writes and reasons with text, and it makes or edits pictures through the image model people keep calling Nano Banana. The grid above hands you both kinds already written, so you copy one, swap in your own photo or topic, and skip the blank-box stare.

What a prompt for Gemini is good at, and where it gets fussy

On the text side Gemini is strong at pulling a long thing down to a short thing. Summarizing a messy email thread, turning rough bullet points into a clean paragraph, explaining a topic at exactly the level you ask for. It can also pull current info because it searches while it answers. Where it gets fussy is when you stack three goals into one breath. Ask it to summarize, then translate, then rewrite in a formal tone, and it will usually quietly drop one of those steps. Split the request and it behaves.

On the image side Nano Banana is at its best editing a photo you already have. Give it a selfie and it can change the light, the background, the outfit, or the whole mood while keeping your face recognizable. Building a brand new scene from words alone works too, but then you carry more of the weight, because you are describing every part of the picture from scratch.

Writing a text prompt for Gemini that gets a usable answer

Most weak text prompts are weak because they leave out the shape of the answer. Gemini cannot tell whether you want two sentences or two pages unless you say so. A reliable pattern is to name the task, give the source or topic, set the length and tone, then say who it is for.

  • Task: summarize, draft, rewrite, explain, compare, or brainstorm. Pick one.
  • Source: paste the actual text, or name the topic clearly.
  • Format: how long, bullets or paragraphs, any sections you want.
  • Audience and tone: for a client, for a kid, casual, formal.

So instead of 'explain quantum computing', try 'explain quantum computing to a curious teenager in about 150 words, no math, with one everyday analogy'. The second one gives Gemini something to actually aim at, and you spend less time re-asking.

Three text prompts worth keeping

If you only save a handful, save these shapes. They cover most of what people use Gemini for day to day, and each one already has the length and the audience baked in.

  1. 'Summarize this in five bullets a manager could read in 30 seconds', then paste the text.
  2. 'Rewrite this message to sound friendly but still professional, same length', then paste your draft.
  3. 'Give me three angles on this topic, each in two sentences, then I will pick one', then name the topic.

Notice none of them ask Gemini to be creative in a vacuum. They give it a job, a size, and a reader. That is the whole trick on the text side.

Image prompts for Gemini and the Nano Banana model

For pictures the rules flip a little. You are art directing now, not asking a question. Tell Gemini the subject, what to keep if you uploaded a photo, the lighting, and the finish you want. Lighting is the word most people forget, and it is the one that turns a flat snapshot into something that looks shot on purpose. Phrases like soft daylight, golden hour, studio softbox, or moody low key all pull real weight.

If you are editing your own photo, the single most useful phrase is telling it what not to touch. Say keep my face exactly and keep the pose, then describe only what should change. That stops Gemini from slowly redrawing you into a stranger who happens to own your shirt.

Tip: when a result is close but not right, do not rewrite the whole prompt. Reply with one correction, like make the background a real cafe instead of a blur, and let Gemini redo just that part.

Photo styles a prompt for Gemini handles well

A lot of the popular requests right now are photo edits you would actually post. The cinematic portrait, with shallow focus and dramatic side light. The retro film look, with grain and faded color, like a scanned photo from the 90s. The 3D figurine or toy version of yourself sitting in its little box. Couple and group edits that stitch two separate photos into one believable scene. And the clean studio product shot, which small shops use for listings. None of these need clever wording. They need you to name the look plainly, then protect your face.

One thing that helps with any of these styles is a reference. If you have seen a look you like, describe it in concrete terms rather than naming a trend that may not mean anything to the model. Saying warm orange and teal color grade, slight film grain, soft window light gets you closer than asking for a viral edit by name. Gemini follows what it can picture, and plain visual words are the easiest thing for it to picture.

Match the prompt for Gemini to what you want to make

This table maps a common goal to the one or two things you should add, and which tool tends to handle it best. Gemini is not always the right answer, and it is fine to admit that.

What you wantAdd to your promptBest tool for it
Edit your own photo, keep your facekeep my face, change only the XGemini (Nano Banana)
Summarize or draft text fastlength, tone, who it is forGemini or ChatGPT
Painterly or stylized art from wordsart style, medium, moodMidjourney
Quick simple graphic from textplain description, one subjectDALL-E or Gemini
Answer that needs fresh factsask it to search and citeGemini

Common prompt for Gemini mistakes, and the quick fix

The most common image complaint is that it changed my face. Move keep my face exactly to the very front of the prompt, run it again, and feed it a clearer source photo. The next complaint is a soft or muddy result, which usually means the original was blurry or you asked for too much in one go. Ask for more detail and contrast, and trim the prompt back to a single change.

On the text side the usual miss is an answer that is too long and too generic. That is almost always a missing length and audience. Add 'in about 100 words, for a busy manager' and the whole thing tightens up. And if Gemini hedges or refuses, it is often because the request was ambiguous, not because it was blocked. Rephrase it plainly and it usually goes through on the next try.

Copy your prompt for Gemini, then make it yours

Treat the prompts above as a starting line, not a finish line. Run one exactly as written first so you can see the baseline. Then change a single slot, the lighting, the length, or the tone, and compare the two. Small moves keep whatever you already liked instead of gambling the whole result on a fresh prompt.

Keep the ones that work in a notes app on your phone. After a week or two you end up with a small personal set of Gemini prompts. One for quick summaries, one for your cinematic selfie edit, one for product shots. At that point you stop hunting for a new example every single time you want the same look.

faqs.q: What is a good prompt for Gemini?
faqs.a: A good one tells Gemini the shape of what you want, not just the topic. For text, name the task, the length, the tone, and who it is for. For images, name the subject, the lighting, and what to keep. Plain instructions beat a long pile of keywords almost every time, and they are far easier to fix later.

faqs.q: What is Nano Banana in Gemini?
faqs.a: Nano Banana is the nickname for Gemini's image model, the part that creates and edits pictures. People use it for portrait edits, retro film looks, figurine versions of themselves, and couple shots. It is strongest at editing a photo you upload, since it can keep your face while changing the light, background, or outfit around it.

faqs.q: How do I keep my face the same when editing a photo in Gemini?
faqs.a: Put a clear instruction like keep my face exactly right at the start of the prompt, then describe only what should change. Use a sharp, well-lit source photo, because a blurry original gives Gemini less to work with. If the face still drifts, run it again and add keep my features and skin tone to lock it down.

faqs.q: Is Gemini better than ChatGPT for prompts?
faqs.a: It depends on the job. For everyday writing, summaries, and questions that need fresh facts, the two are close, and Gemini's live search helps. For editing a real photo while keeping your face, Gemini's image model is the easier pick. For painterly art from a pure description, many people still reach for Midjourney instead.

faqs.q: Why does Gemini give me such long answers?
faqs.a: Usually because the prompt never set a length. Gemini fills the space it is given, so add something like in about 80 words or three short bullets. Naming the audience helps too, since for a busy manager pushes it to cut fluff. A length plus an audience fixes most overlong, generic replies in one shot.
